From Hippocrates to Baghdad to Delhi: 2,400 years of the “Greek medicine”.

400 BCE · Four humours in the body (Hippocrates and his followers (the treatise is often credited to his son-in-law Polybus))
170 · Galen builds the system (Galen of Pergamon)
830 · The House of Wisdom translates the Greeks (Scholars of the Abbasid caliphs, especially under al-Ma’mun (r. 813–833))
900 · A doctor who kept notes (Abu Bakr al-Razi (Rhazes))
1025 · The Canon of Medicine (Ibn Sina (Avicenna))
1206 · Hakims come to India (Physicians of the Delhi Sultanate)

captions.instagram:
How does Unani medicine work?

Unani means “Greek”: a 2,400-year-old system that travelled from Hippocrates to Baghdad to Delhi. Follow Ibn Sina’s Canon across a map, move a patient’s mizaj across the hot–cold, moist–dry board, work out the suction in a hijama cup, and run a fair trial to see what the evidence really says.

→ Unani means “Greek”: it began with Hippocrates and Galen and their four body fluids.
→ Baghdad translated it, Ibn Sina organised it in 1025, and it took root in India.
→ Unani describes four humours: blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile.
→ Their mix is your mizaj, and six everyday factors are said to tip the balance.
→ A hakim reads the pulse; in hijama, air cooling in a sealed cup sucks up the skin.

youtubeLong.title: How does Unani medicine work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Unani means “Greek”: a 2,400-year-old system that travelled from Hippocrates to Baghdad to Delhi. Follow Ibn Sina’s Canon across a map, move a patient’s mizaj across the hot–cold, moist–dry board, work out the suction in a hijama cup, and run a fair trial to see what the evidence really says.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/e/unaniclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/unaniclear

In this video:
• From Greece to Baghdad to Delhi. Unani grew from the Greek medicine of Hippocrates and Galen.
• Four humours, one temperament. In its own terms, Unani says the body holds four humours, dam, balgham, safra and sauda, whose mix sets your mizaj: hot or cold, moist or dry.
• Pulse, flask, cup and jar. A hakim reads the pulse (nabz), looks at urine in a flask (qaroora) and asks about your life.
• What history got right and wrong. Ibn Sina’s Canon set out rules for testing a medicine and described diseases that pass between people.
• What the evidence says. Only a fair test, randomised, blinded and placebo-controlled, can show if a remedy works.
• Using it wisely. Never stop prescribed medicine, tell every doctor and hakim what you take, and see a qualified doctor for serious illness.
